cards.title: Trump Risks Trading Taiwan Security and Tech Access for a Fragile U.S.-China Trade Truce
cards.background: U.S. President Donald Trump arrived in Beijing on Wednesday for a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, with trade set to dominate the agenda. The White House is seeking new deals to cut the U.S. trade deficit and is expected to prioritize a rare-earths truce and market access for American tech firms, including AI companies. In October, Washington said Beijing agreed to effectively eliminate export controls on rare earth elements in exchange for reduced U.S. tariffs, but Chinese customs data still shows exports of several critical resources remain roughly 50 percent below pre-April 2025 levels. Xi is also expected to press Trump on Taiwan, after Washington announced an $11.1 billion arms sale to Taipei in December.

prop_args.thesis: A trade-first summit is rational because it can secure immediate economic gains and reduce the risk of a broader U.S.-China escalation.
mechanisms: First, prioritizing trade can lock in a rare-earths supply truce. This is because (1) China still dominates the production of several critical resources, (2) exports remain about 50 percent below pre-control levels, and (3) U.S. industries from defense to electronics are exposed to supply shocks if Beijing reimposes controls.

Second, a deal on market access and tariffs can deliver visible domestic wins for Trump. Three reasons: one, the White House is explicitly trying to reduce the trade deficit; two, lower tariffs can ease consumer price pressure in the U.S.; three, business leaders like Jensen Huang, Tim Cook, Elon Musk, and Kelly Ortberg signal that major firms want stability more than confrontation.

Third, narrowing the summit to economics lowers the chance of a security spiral. This matters because (1) if both sides can claim a win on trade, there is less incentive to escalate over Taiwan or tech export controls, (2) predictable commercial ties create channels for future bargaining, and (3) even a limited truce can buy time for U.S. firms to adapt supply chains.

opp_args.thesis: Putting trade above security invites strategic concession and weakens U.S. leverage against China.
mechanisms: First, Trump may trade away Taiwan support for short-term economic gains. One, Xi has a clear incentive to demand delayed or reduced arms deliveries to Taipei; two, Trump has already signaled openness by saying he will discuss whether the U.S. should still sell weapons to Taiwan; three, any perceived softening undermines deterrence because Beijing learns coercion can buy concessions.

Second, a trade-only approach rewards Chinese coercive leverage rather than changing it. One, China has already used rare-earth export controls as pressure; two, if the U.S. responds by bargaining for partial relief instead of imposing costs, Beijing learns that supply-chain chokepoints are effective tools; three, this encourages future economic blackmail in other sectors like AI chips and critical minerals.

Third, opening Chinese markets to U.S. tech can accelerate China’s long-term competitiveness. One, American firms may transfer know-how, standards, and ecosystem advantages into China; two, China already has cost advantages in AI deployment and scale; three, any short-term export or sales win may strengthen a strategic rival that can later outcompete U.S. firms globally.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the summit produces durable economic stability or merely purchases short-term calm at the cost of strategic leverage. Pro-trade wins if you prioritize immediate supply-chain relief and domestic price effects; opposition wins if you think concessions on Taiwan and tech create irreversible security and competitiveness losses.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would prioritize trade over security concerns in negotiations with China
THBT the United States should trade market access for Chinese concessions on rare earths
THP a world where major powers can de-escalate rivalry through economic deals rather than security commitments

cards.title: Trump–Xi Summit Trades Taiwan and Tech Access for a Fragile U.S.-China Economic Truce
cards.background: Donald Trump arrived in Beijing on May 13, 2026, ahead of a summit with Xi Jinping the next day. The talks are expected to focus on extending a fragile truce over Chinese rare earth exports, with the White House having said in October that Beijing agreed to “effectively eliminate” current and proposed export controls on rare earth elements in exchange for reduced U.S. tariff threats. The summit is also expected to cover artificial intelligence market access and Taiwan, including Washington’s $11.1 billion arms sale to Taipei announced in December.

prop_args.thesis: A transactional summit can stabilize the world’s two largest economies by reducing immediate trade and supply-chain shocks.
mechanisms: First, a rare-earths deal lowers the risk of sudden industrial bottlenecks. This is because (1) China dominates critical mineral processing and export controls can instantly hit U.S. manufacturing, (2) the October truce already shows both sides can trade concessions for predictability, and (3) keeping flows open protects sectors like EVs, semiconductors, and defense supply chains from price spikes and delays.

Second, limited market-opening on AI can improve efficiency and growth on both sides. Three reasons: one, U.S. firms gain access to the world’s largest consumer market, two, Chinese firms face stronger competition and technology diffusion, and three, cross-border commercial ties create constituencies that prefer stability over escalation.

Third, de-escalating on Taiwan in exchange for economic gains can reduce the chance of accidental crisis. This matters because even if the underlying dispute remains, delaying arms deliveries or softening rhetoric can buy time, lower signaling intensity, and prevent a trade summit from collapsing into broader strategic confrontation.

opp_args.thesis: A deal built on concessions over Taiwan and tech access rewards coercion and makes future Chinese pressure more effective.
mechanisms: First, it normalizes hostage diplomacy. (1) If Beijing learns it can extract trade or market-access concessions by threatening rare-earth supply or escalating on Taiwan, (2) it has stronger incentives to repeat the tactic, and (3) the U.S. becomes more vulnerable in every future negotiation.

Second, short-term economic relief can weaken long-term strategic competition. (1) Allowing major U.S. tech companies into China risks forced spillovers, data exposure, and regulatory capture, (2) delaying arms deliveries to Taiwan undermines deterrence by signaling wavering U.S. commitment, and (3) the result is a more confident China facing a more divided U.S. coalition.

Third, the deal may be unstable because the underlying conflict is structural, not transactional. (1) Rare-earth dependence, AI rivalry, and Taiwan are all tied to core national-security interests, (2) any side can renege once it gets what it wants, and (3) the summit could therefore produce only temporary calm while increasing the odds of a larger future rupture.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether immediate economic stability outweighs the long-term cost of legitimizing coercive leverage. Prop wins if the judge prioritizes supply-chain continuity and crisis avoidance; opp wins if they think concessions on Taiwan and tech create a more dangerous strategic equilibrium that is harder to reverse.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would prioritize trade détente with China over Taiwan signaling
THBT the United States should trade market access for Chinese cooperation on rare earth exports
THP a world where U.S.-China economic competition is managed through summit-level bargains
THBT states should not use Taiwan as leverage in broader economic negotiations with China

cards.title: India Uses BRICS to Hedge Against the West, but Bloc Expansion Risks Paralysis
cards.background: India is hosting the BRICS foreign ministers’ meeting in New Delhi on Thursday and Friday as chair of the bloc, with the annual leaders’ summit due in September. BRICS has expanded beyond the original five members to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, and the UAE, while Saudi Arabia also participates in BRICS activities. The article notes that the 2024 BRICS leaders’ summit in Russia drew representatives from 35 countries and several international organizations, but the bloc’s consensus model is now under strain from conflicts among new members, especially Iran-UAE and Egypt-Ethiopia tensions, as well as the Iran war.

prop_args.thesis: India’s continued backing of BRICS is strategically rational because it gives New Delhi leverage to hedge between the West and the non-West while preserving autonomy in a more fragmented world.
mechanisms: First, BRICS gives India a coalition platform without formal alliance costs. This is because (1) India can deepen ties with the West while still engaging Russia, Iran, the Gulf, and other Global South states, (2) the bloc’s broad membership lets India avoid binary alignment in U.S.-China competition, and (3) India can extract diplomatic prestige by chairing a forum that includes major regional powers and attracts wider attendance.

Second, BRICS advances Indian foreign-policy priorities that the West has historically under-delivered on. Three reasons: one, it keeps UN reform and Global South representation on the agenda; two, it creates space to discuss sanctions circumvention and alternative financial architecture; three, it lets India present itself as a leader of the developing world rather than a junior partner in Western-led institutions.

Third, BRICS expansion actually helps India if it dilutes anti-Western cohesion. This matters because (1) most new members besides Iran are also aligned with the West, (2) that makes BRICS less likely to become an overt anti-American bloc, and (3) a looser, more plural forum is ideal for India, which wants access and flexibility rather than ideological discipline.

opp_args.thesis: India should stop overinvesting in BRICS because the bloc’s expansion and internal rivalries now make it a low-yield forum that can damage India’s credibility without delivering concrete gains.
mechanisms: First, BRICS consensus politics create paralysis rather than power. One, the new members have direct conflicts such as Iran versus the UAE and Egypt versus Ethiopia; two, consensus means any one member can block substantive outcomes; three, this makes joint statements vague and prevents real institutional progress like a BRICS bank or coordinated policy.

Second, India’s association with BRICS increasingly creates diplomatic downside with the West. One, even if India does not intend BRICS to be anti-Western, the bloc is still framed as a challenger to U.S.-led order; two, Trump’s threat of 100 percent tariffs shows the West may respond coercively to BRICS symbolism; three, India risks being caught in retaliatory politics despite not sharing the most radical members’ goals.

Third, BRICS can entangle India in conflicts and rivalries it cannot manage. One, India’s relations with Iran are fragile because of its growing ties with the UAE and Saudi Arabia; two, the Iran war can derail summit outcomes and force India to mediate disputes it cannot solve; three, if India cannot deliver a substantive summit, it weakens New Delhi’s image as a competent convenor.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether BRICS is a strategic hedge or a reputational trap. Prop wins if the round is about autonomy and optionality in a multipolar order; opp wins if the judge prioritizes concrete institutional output and the costs of being tied to a dysfunctional, increasingly politicized bloc.
motion_areas: TH, as India, would continue to prioritize BRICS membership and leadership
THBT middle powers should hedge through blocs like BRICS rather than align with the West
THP a world in which BRICS becomes a major alternative forum to Western-led institutions

cards.title: US-China Summit Becomes a Test of Whether AI Rivalry Overrides Trade and Iran Cooperation
cards.background: US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are scheduled to meet on Thursday morning in Beijing, according to the White House. Bloomberg reports the summit is expected to focus heavily on trade and the war in Iran, while tensions over artificial intelligence also loom over the talks. The meeting comes at a moment of heightened strategic competition between Washington and Beijing, with both sides weighing whether to cooperate on immediate crises or intensify rivalry over advanced technology.

prop_args.thesis: The summit will push the US and China toward a more explicit technology containment regime, because AI competition is now inseparable from military and economic power.
mechanisms: First, AI is a dual-use technology, so any concession in the summit is read as a security concession. This is because (1) frontier models can improve intelligence, targeting, cyber operations, and autonomous systems, (2) export controls on chips and compute become national security tools rather than commercial policy, and (3) both governments face domestic pressure to avoid appearing weak on strategic technology.

Second, the summit incentivizes decoupling in the most sensitive parts of the AI stack. Three reasons: one, the US can use the meeting to justify tighter limits on advanced semiconductors, cloud access, and model training infrastructure; two, China can respond by accelerating indigenous substitution and restricting market access for US firms; three, once firms anticipate political risk, they re-route supply chains and investment away from cross-border dependence.

Third, this matters because AI rivalry spills into broader geopolitical bargaining. This is because (1) if each side believes the other can gain battlefield or surveillance advantages from AI, compromise on trade becomes harder, (2) technology disputes poison trust needed for coordination on Iran, and (3) the result is a durable bloc structure where economic interdependence is subordinated to security competition.

opp_args.thesis: The summit will moderate AI tensions because both sides need limited cooperation to avoid escalation and preserve economic stability.
mechanisms: First, leaders have incentives to compartmentalize AI from the rest of the relationship. One, Trump and Xi can frame AI as a managed competition issue rather than a crisis trigger; two, both economies still benefit from trade and investment flows that would be damaged by a full tech rupture; three, summit diplomacy often produces signaling commitments even when underlying rivalry remains.

Second, immediate geopolitical crises like the war in Iran can crowd out maximalist AI confrontation. One, both governments may prioritize deconfliction and crisis management over symbolic tech escalation; two, shared interest in preventing wider regional instability creates room for pragmatic bargaining; three, when the agenda is dominated by urgent security issues, AI becomes a secondary file that is easier to postpone or soften.

Third, limited cooperation can reduce the risk of an uncontrolled arms race. One, dialogue on AI safety, standards, and incident prevention lowers misperception; two, even adversaries can agree on guardrails for military use and export enforcement; three, preserving channels of communication is better for both sides than forcing a zero-sum race that raises the chance of accidental escalation.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether AI is treated as a narrow bargaining chip or a core national-security frontier. Prop wins if you believe strategic distrust dominates and turns every summit into a step toward decoupling; opp wins if you think leaders can compartmentalize and use summit diplomacy to slow escalation without resolving rivalry.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would prioritize AI containment over trade concessions in negotiations with China
THBT major powers should treat frontier AI as a national security issue rather than a commercial one
THP a world where US-China summit diplomacy is used to manage AI rivalry
TH, as China, would retaliate against US AI export controls with reciprocal technology restrictions

cards.title: US-China AI Safety Cooperation Becomes a Strategic Necessity Amid Great-Power Rivalry
cards.background: The article is framed around the argument that the US should engage China on AI safety before strategic competition makes cooperation impossible. The only concrete event in the provided text is the first face-to-face meeting in six years between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping on October 30, 2025, held at Gimhae Air Base in Busan, where the two leaders sought a truce to end a trade war that had roiled the world economy. The piece situates AI safety within broader US-China rivalry, implying that the window for bilateral coordination is narrowing as competition intensifies.

prop_args.thesis: The US should engage China on AI safety now because cooperation is the only realistic way to reduce catastrophic miscalculation in a domain where both sides are racing ahead.
mechanisms: First, bilateral engagement creates minimum safety standards before competitive pressure hardens into an uncontrolled arms race. This is because (1) both states have incentives to deploy models quickly for military and economic advantage, (2) unilateral restraint is fragile when the other side can free-ride, and (3) even limited talks can establish red lines around model testing, deployment, and incident reporting.

Second, engagement reduces the risk of accidental escalation from AI-enabled military or cyber systems. Three reasons: one, AI systems can compress decision time and increase the chance of false positives in crisis settings; two, shared protocols for attribution and emergency communication lower the odds that a technical failure becomes a geopolitical incident; three, regular contact builds trust channels that matter most during a fast-moving crisis.

Third, cooperation is strategically valuable because it preserves US leadership over the rules of the game. This matters because if Washington refuses to engage, Beijing can frame itself as the responsible actor, attract third-country support for its standards, and lock in norms that the US later has to accept rather than shape.

opp_args.thesis: The US should avoid deep AI safety engagement with China because it risks transferring strategic knowledge while giving Beijing diplomatic cover without meaningful restraint.
mechanisms: First, talks can become a channel for intelligence leakage and capability signaling. One, AI safety discussions often require disclosure of model architecture, testing methods, or compute governance practices; two, China can use that information to benchmark its own systems and accelerate military applications; three, the US may end up revealing more than it gains because verification in this space is weak.

Second, engagement can legitimize a rival that is structurally unlikely to comply. One, China has incentives to sign symbolic agreements while continuing opaque military-civil fusion efforts; two, weak enforcement means commitments are hard to monitor and easy to violate; three, the US may soften allied pressure by creating the appearance of progress without actual constraint.

Third, cooperation may blunt deterrence by signaling that the US sees AI as a shared governance issue rather than a competitive domain. This matters because (1) Beijing may interpret dialogue as evidence that Washington fears escalation and wants accommodation, (2) that reduces pressure on China to slow deployment, and (3) it can embolden more aggressive experimentation under the cover of diplomacy.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether AI risk is primarily a coordination problem or a security problem. Pro side wins if the round prioritizes catastrophic downside and the need for even imperfect guardrails; opposition wins if they prove engagement is non-verifiable, strategically leaky, and mostly symbolic.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would pursue bilateral AI safety talks with China
THBT great powers should cooperate on AI safety even amid strategic rivalry
THP a world where the US and China establish formal AI incident hotlines and safety protocols

cards.title: U.S.-Iran Standoff in the Strait of Hormuz Threatens Global Energy Security and Regional Escalation
cards.region: Strait of Hormuz / United States / Iran
cards.background: NPR reports that the United States and Iran are deadlocked over the Strait of Hormuz, with neither side willing to back down. The Strait is one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints, carrying a large share of global oil and liquefied natural gas exports from the Gulf. The article frames the situation as unresolved and potentially dangerous, but provides no further operational details in the text supplied.

prop_args.thesis: A firm U.S. posture in the Strait of Hormuz is necessary to deter Iranian coercion and preserve the credibility of the global maritime order.
mechanisms: First, deterrence only works if Iran believes disruption will be met with costs. This is because (1) the Strait is a narrow chokepoint where even limited harassment can create outsized market panic, (2) if the U.S. signals hesitation, Iran can test red lines incrementally without triggering a response, and (3) repeated unpunished brinkmanship normalizes coercion and makes future threats cheaper to execute.

Second, U.S. resolve protects the wider shipping system from becoming hostage to regional revisionism. Three reasons: one, the Strait is not just a bilateral issue but a global commons for energy transit; two, allies in Europe and Asia depend on predictable Gulf flows and U.S. security guarantees; three, allowing Iran to dictate access would encourage other states to weaponize chokepoints in their own regions.

Third, even if tensions rise in the short term, credibility and stability improve over time when the U.S. demonstrates it will defend freedom of navigation. This matters because a one-time show of weakness can produce a long-run equilibrium of higher insurance costs, rerouted trade, and more frequent crises.

opp_args.thesis: Escalatory U.S. pressure in the Strait of Hormuz is more likely to provoke conflict and economic shock than to restore stability.
mechanisms: First, military brinkmanship creates a classic escalation ladder. One, the Strait is so strategically sensitive that even minor incidents can be misread as preparation for attack; two, both sides have incentives to save face, making de-escalation politically costly; three, once assets are deployed, commanders on the ground have less room to avoid accidental clashes.

Second, the economic costs of confrontation are immediate and global, while the supposed deterrent benefits are uncertain. One, oil and shipping markets react within hours to perceived risk, raising prices and insurance premiums; two, import-dependent states bear the cost even if no shots are fired; three, those costs can outlast the crisis and weaken the broader world economy.

Third, hardline U.S. policy can strengthen Iranian domestic hardliners and reduce the chance of diplomacy. This is because (1) external pressure lets Tehran frame compromise as capitulation, (2) moderates lose leverage when security threats dominate politics, and (3) sanctions-plus-threats often entrench the very regime behavior they aim to change.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether resolve prevents future coercion or whether it triggers immediate escalation in a chokepoint where small incidents have global consequences. Prop wins if the round is about long-run order and deterrence; Opp wins if the round prioritizes the high probability of accidental war and the certainty of short-term economic harm.

THBT the West should prioritize freedom of navigation over de-escalation in the Persian Gulf
THP a world where the U.S. credibly threatens force to protect maritime chokepoints
THBT states should not negotiate under threats to global energy shipping

cards.title: Iran’s Detention of British Nationals Turns Consular Risk Into a Coercive Hostage Tool
cards.background: Lindsay Foreman and Craig Foreman, both 53 and from East Sussex, were arrested in January 2025 while travelling through Iran on an around-the-world motorcycle trip. They were sentenced to 10 years in Tehran’s Evin prison on espionage charges, which they deny. Their family says they have now lost contact after phone access — their only link to the outside world — was cut off earlier this month, reportedly after the couple gave a media interview about their detention. The UK Foreign Office says it withdrew staff from Iran in February due to the threat of US strikes and continues to warn that British nationals face a 'significant risk of arrest, questioning or detention' and that British links alone can be enough for detention.

prop_args.thesis: The UK should treat arbitrary detention of its nationals in Iran as a coercive hostage strategy and respond with maximal diplomatic, legal, and travel-cost escalation rather than quiet consular management.
mechanisms: First, escalation raises the expected cost of detention for Tehran. This is because (1) Iran uses foreign detainees as bargaining chips to extract concessions, publicity, or silence, (2) private diplomacy alone signals that the UK will absorb the abuse without imposing counter-costs, and (3) public, coordinated pressure makes the detention less useful as leverage because it increases reputational and diplomatic damage every day the prisoners remain isolated.

Second, a hardline response protects future travellers and dual nationals by changing the incentive structure. Three reasons: one, if Iran learns that detaining British citizens triggers sanctions, travel advisories, and multilateral pressure, it becomes less attractive to target them; two, the current warning that a British passport can itself be enough for detention shows the problem is systemic, not isolated; three, visible punishment creates deterrence beyond this case and reduces the pool of vulnerable hostages.

Third, this is a rule-of-law and human-rights issue, not just a bilateral dispute. This matters because (1) the couple were sentenced on espionage charges they deny, (2) cutting off phone access after they spoke publicly looks like retaliation for speech and contact with the outside world, and (3) if democracies do not respond strongly to arbitrary detention, authoritarian states learn they can isolate detainees, deny due process, and still keep normal relations.

opp_args.thesis: The UK should prioritize quiet diplomacy and consular bargaining because public escalation is more likely to harden Iran’s position and worsen the couple’s treatment.
mechanisms: First, public pressure can trigger retaliation against the detainees. One, the family says phone access was cut after the couple gave a media interview, which suggests Tehran already punishes visibility; two, if the UK escalates publicly, Iran can respond by further restricting contact, access to lawyers, food, or medical care; three, the prisoners are physically inside Evin prison, so the state has immediate control over their welfare.

Second, Iran is more likely to release detainees through discreet bargaining than through humiliation. One, hostage diplomacy usually works through back-channel deals, prisoner swaps, or quiet concessions; two, public confrontation makes it harder for Iranian leaders to save face domestically; three, if the regime feels cornered, it may prefer to keep the couple as leverage rather than concede under pressure.

Third, the UK has limited leverage and should avoid symbolic escalation that does not change outcomes. One, the Foreign Office has already withdrawn staff from Iran, reducing on-the-ground capacity; two, broad sanctions or rhetoric may satisfy domestic audiences but do little to alter Tehran’s calculus; three, the immediate priority is the couple’s safety, and the least risky route is the one least likely to provoke further punishment.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether pressure improves the couple’s chances or simply increases the risk of retaliation inside Evin prison. Prop wins if the round is about deterrence and state credibility; opp wins if the judge prioritizes immediate prisoner welfare and believes Tehran responds mainly to quiet bargaining.

cards.title: Trump’s China Summit Opens a High-Stakes Bargain Over Trade, Security, and Alliance Credibility
cards.background: Bloomberg’s Balance of Power episode on 13 May 2026 centers on President Donald Trump’s trip to China for a summit with Xi Jinping. The segment features discussion from former State Department Chief Economist Chad Bown, Maywood Strategies Principal Douglas Farrar, Stonecourt Capital Partner Rick Davis, Democratic Congresswoman Suzan DelBene, and American Action Forum President Douglas Holtz-Eakin. The article itself is a show description rather than a substantive policy report, so the debate value comes from the summit context: direct US-China leader-level talks at a moment of elevated trade, security, and alliance tensions.

prop_args.thesis: A Trump-Xi summit is useful because direct leader-level bargaining can produce immediate de-escalation and transactional deals that lower the risk of a broader US-China confrontation.
mechanisms: First, face-to-face summitry creates a credible off-ramp from escalation. This is because (1) both leaders can trade symbolic concessions without domestic bureaucracies slowing them down, (2) personal commitment signals can reduce misperception and accidental escalation, and (3) a public summit gives each side political cover to pause tariffs, export controls, or military signaling.

Second, the summit can unlock narrow but economically meaningful bargains. Three reasons: one, China and the US can separate headline rivalry from sector-specific issues like agriculture, semiconductors, and market access; two, a leader-level deal can instruct agencies to implement follow-through faster than normal diplomacy; three, even partial agreements stabilize expectations for firms and investors, reducing volatility in supply chains and capital markets.

Third, the strategic value is in buying time, not solving rivalry. This matters because a managed competition framework is preferable to uncontrolled confrontation: even if the summit does not end structural competition, it can preserve communication channels, reduce the chance of crisis spirals, and keep the relationship within a controllable diplomatic lane.

opp_args.thesis: A Trump-Xi summit is more likely to weaken US leverage and normalize coercive Chinese behavior than to produce durable gains.
mechanisms: First, summitry rewards China for waiting out pressure. One, Beijing can offer small, reversible concessions in exchange for major US symbolic recognition; two, this teaches China that escalation followed by negotiation works better than compliance; three, it undermines the credibility of US threats because tariffs or restrictions become bargaining chips rather than enforcement tools.

Second, the deal structure is likely to be shallow and unstable. One, the core disputes are structural—technology transfer, industrial policy, military competition, and Taiwan—so they cannot be solved in one meeting; two, any agreement is vulnerable to domestic backlash in Washington or Beijing, making implementation fragile; three, markets and allies may overread temporary calm as real resolution, leading to strategic complacency.

Third, the summit can damage alliance confidence. One, allies may fear the US will cut bilateral side deals that ignore their security concerns; two, if Trump appears willing to trade away pressure on China for short-term wins, partners hedge by pursuing independent arrangements; three, that weakens the broader coalition needed to constrain Chinese power over the long run.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between immediate crisis management and long-term strategic credibility. Prop wins if the round prioritizes preventing escalation and preserving channels; Opp wins if the judge thinks summitry mainly produces shallow concessions that erode deterrence and alliance trust.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would pursue a leader-level summit with China despite ongoing strategic rivalry
THBT the US should prioritize direct summit diplomacy over coercive economic pressure in managing China
THP a world where major-power disputes are handled through frequent leader summits rather than bureaucratic channels

cards.title: Trump’s Iran War Tests Congress’s Power to Stop Unauthorised Military Escalation
cards.background: On 13 May 2026, the US Senate rejected a war powers resolution by a 49-50 vote, marking the seventh Democratic attempt to force an end to American involvement in the war on Iran since the conflict began in February. All Democrats except John Fetterman supported the measure, and for the first time Alaska Republican Lisa Murkowski voted in favor, joining Rand Paul and Susan Collins as the only Republicans backing it. Congress has not formally authorized the campaign, while the Trump administration argues that a ceasefire with Iran means the 60-day deadline under the 1973 War Powers Act no longer applies.

prop_args.thesis: Congress should be able to stop an undeclared war when the executive branch expands a conflict without formal authorization.
mechanisms: First, this restores constitutional checks on war-making. This is because (1) the War Powers Act was designed to stop presidents from unilaterally dragging the country into sustained hostilities, (2) repeated Senate votes show there is no durable legislative consent for the campaign, and (3) forcing a vote creates a public accountability moment that can constrain future executive escalation.

Second, it reduces the risk of mission creep and strategic overreach. Three reasons: one, once troops and strikes are already underway, presidents have incentives to keep escalating to avoid looking weak; two, Congress is better placed to force a debate on end goals, exit conditions, and costs; three, the absence of an AUMF means the war can continue by inertia rather than by democratic choice.

Third, it improves long-run US credibility and alliance management. This matters because allies and adversaries both read congressional authorization as a signal of domestic durability; if the war is politically contested at home, a forced stop can prevent the US from committing to an open-ended conflict it may later abandon, which is worse for deterrence than a deliberate pause.

opp_args.thesis: Stopping the war through a war powers resolution would prematurely constrain the president and risk leaving the US without a coherent strategy against Iran.
mechanisms: First, it can undercut active military operations before they achieve their objectives. One, the administration says a ceasefire is in place, so the conflict is in a fluid transition rather than a clean peace; two, pulling support mid-operation can expose US forces and partners to retaliation; three, Congress may not have a workable alternative plan for deterrence, containment, or enforcement.

Second, it can weaken crisis bargaining and embolden Iran. One, if Tehran sees Congress unwilling to sustain pressure, it may conclude the US lacks resolve; two, adversaries can exploit legislative division to wait out American commitments; three, a premature cutoff may reduce leverage in any follow-on AUMF or ceasefire framework.

Third, the proper remedy is authorization, not abrupt termination. One, Murkowski and others argue for a future AUMF, which suggests Congress can regularize the war without immediately ending it; two, a tailored authorization can set objectives, limits, and reporting requirements; three, this preserves democratic oversight while avoiding the operational shock of an immediate shutdown.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between democratic control and operational continuity. Prop wins if the round prioritizes constitutional legitimacy and preventing open-ended executive war, while Opp wins if the judge thinks the immediate costs of halting an ongoing conflict outweigh the abstract harm of unauthorized force.

THBT legislatures should be able to terminate ongoing military operations launched without prior authorization
THP a world where war powers resolutions can automatically suspend undeclared conflicts after 60 days

cards.title: US Supreme Court Weakens Voting Rights Act, Triggering a Mid-Decade Gerrymander Arms Race in Georgia and the South
cards.background: Georgia Republican governor Brian Kemp announced a special legislative session starting 17 June to redraw state legislative and congressional maps. The move comes after the US supreme court’s April ruling in Louisiana v Callais, which effectively weakened Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act by striking down districts drawn to protect Black and minority voting power as unconstitutional racial gerrymanders. Georgia is joining a broader mid-decade redistricting wave already seen in Louisiana, Alabama, Tennessee, and other states, with some maps being redrawn before the 2026 elections.

prop_args.thesis: The Supreme Court’s ruling and Georgia’s redraw entrench majority rule over minority representation, making the political system less democratic and more durable for one party.
mechanisms: First, the new legal environment lowers the cost of partisan map manipulation. This is because (1) states can now justify aggressive redistricting as compliance with anti-racial-gerrymandering doctrine, (2) Republican-controlled legislatures can move quickly while they still hold unified power, and (3) once maps are locked in, they shape multiple election cycles rather than one contest.

Second, the redraw can directly eliminate minority-preferred seats and weaken Black political voice. Three reasons: one, the article notes Republicans could draw Democratic Rep. Sanford Bishop, a Black member of Congress since 1993, out of his seat; two, similar moves in Louisiana, Alabama, and Tennessee already targeted Black-majority districts; three, removing such districts reduces the number of candidates who can win by mobilizing minority communities rather than relying on white crossover votes.

Third, this creates a self-reinforcing partisan arms race that advantages the side with state power. This matters because (1) each redraw pressures the other party to retaliate in kind, (2) the result is a national escalation of mid-decade gerrymandering outside the normal census cycle, and (3) over time the party that controls more state governments can convert temporary electoral advantage into structural House-seat advantage.

opp_args.thesis: Redistricting is a legitimate response to a changed legal framework and can improve representational fairness by aligning maps with current law and population realities.
mechanisms: First, the Supreme Court’s decision forces states to update maps to avoid unconstitutional racial classifications. One, states cannot keep using districts that courts may now strike down; two, redrawing avoids litigation uncertainty and election chaos; three, legislatures have a duty to implement the new legal standard rather than freeze outdated maps in place.

Second, partisan map changes do not necessarily translate into durable control because aggressive gerrymanders can backfire. One, the article explicitly notes the risk of a 'dummymander' where overreach helps the opposition; two, demographic and turnout shifts can make supposedly safe seats competitive; three, courts, ballot measures, and state-level resistance can still constrain the most extreme plans.

Third, the process can be defended as restoring accountability in a polarized system. One, if districts are drawn to reflect current political geography, voters get clearer responsibility for outcomes; two, states like South Carolina have shown that not every Republican state will follow Trump-style pressure, so the national effect is not uniform; three, mid-decade redraws may simply be a temporary correction rather than a permanent democratic collapse.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the redraw is treated as lawful compliance or as strategic entrenchment. Prop is stronger on structural impact because once minority districts are removed and maps are locked in, the harm compounds across several election cycles, while Opp mostly relies on uncertainty, legal necessity, and the possibility of a dummymander.

THBT US states should be allowed to redraw electoral maps mid-decade
THP a world where independent commissions control all congressional redistricting
THBT the Democratic Party should respond to Republican gerrymanders in kind

cards.title: Warsh’s Narrow Fed Confirmation Raises the Risk of Political Capture at the U.S. Central Bank
cards.background: On Wednesday, the U.S. Senate confirmed Kevin Warsh as chair of the Federal Reserve by a 54-45 vote, the narrowest confirmation margin ever for a central bank chief. The vote came amid intense partisan polarization and Democratic concern that Warsh will be more willing to cut interest rates quickly in line with President Donald Trump’s demands. The confirmation sets up a major test of the Federal Reserve’s independence at a time when monetary policy remains politically salient.

prop_args.thesis: A politically aligned Fed chair undermines monetary credibility, making the U.S. economy more vulnerable to inflation, asset bubbles, and long-run instability.
mechanisms: First, political pressure to cut rates too quickly weakens the Fed’s inflation-fighting credibility. This is because (1) markets start to believe policy is being set for electoral convenience rather than macroeconomic fundamentals, (2) wage- and price-setters then expect higher future inflation and adjust behavior accordingly, and (3) the Fed must eventually tighten harder to restore credibility, causing a sharper slowdown later.

Second, a chair seen as responsive to the White House lowers borrowing costs in the short term but encourages excess risk-taking. Three reasons: one, cheaper credit inflates equities, housing, and private credit valuations; two, firms and households take on more leverage under the assumption rates will stay artificially low; three, when inflation or financial stress returns, the correction is larger because leverage has built up across the economy.

Third, preserving central bank independence matters because it is one of the few institutional checks on executive overreach in economic policy. This matters because the Fed can absorb politically unpopular tightening now to prevent a worse recession or inflation spike later, whereas a captured Fed tends to prioritize short-term growth optics over long-term price stability.

opp_args.thesis: A more responsive Fed chair can better align monetary policy with real economic conditions and democratic accountability, especially when the central bank has become too insulated from public pressure.
mechanisms: First, the Fed is not politically neutral in practice, so greater responsiveness can correct a bias toward overly tight policy. One, central bankers can become institutionally conservative and overvalue inflation avoidance relative to employment; two, elected leaders face broader macroeconomic mandates from voters, including jobs and growth; three, if the economy is slowing, faster rate cuts can prevent unnecessary unemployment and business failures.

Second, a chair who can work with the administration may reduce policy gridlock and improve macro coordination. One, fiscal and monetary policy are more effective when they are not pulling in opposite directions; two, clearer alignment can stabilize expectations if markets believe the government is pursuing a coherent growth strategy; three, in a crisis or softening cycle, speed matters more than abstract independence.

Third, fears of capture may be overstated because the Fed still has institutional constraints and market discipline. One, the FOMC is a committee, not a one-person monarchy; two, bond markets and inflation data punish reckless easing quickly; three, if Warsh cuts too aggressively, rising yields and inflation expectations will force a correction regardless of presidential preferences.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether central bank independence is a hard constraint that prevents macroeconomic abuse, or an elite norm that can be traded off for faster growth and employment. Prop wins if you prioritize credibility and the long-run inflation/unemployment tradeoff; Opp wins if you believe the Fed has become too cautious and that democratic responsiveness improves policy timing without fully eliminating institutional checks.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would prioritize central bank independence over democratic responsiveness
THBT the Federal Reserve should be insulated from presidential influence
THP a world where central bank chairs are selected primarily for policy alignment with the elected government

cards.title: Secret Israel-UAE Wartime Coordination Turns the Abraham Accords Into a De Facto Anti-Iran Security Alliance
cards.region: Israel / United Arab Emirates / Iran / Middle East-Gulf
cards.background: Benjamin Netanyahu revealed he made a secret trip to the UAE on 26 March 2026, meeting UAE president Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Al Ain during the Iran war. Reuters also reported that Mossad chief David Barnea made at least two visits to the UAE during the conflict to coordinate military actions. On Tuesday, US ambassador Mike Huckabee said Israel had shared its air defence system with the UAE, including Iron Dome batteries and military specialists, while the Wall Street Journal reported the UAE conducted its own strikes on Iran, including an attack on a refinery on Lavan island in early April.

prop_args.thesis: The secret Netanyahu visit shows the Abraham Accords are evolving from symbolic normalization into a real regional security bloc that can deter Iran and reduce Gulf states' dependence on the US.
mechanisms: First, the visit institutionalizes intelligence and military coordination between Israel and the UAE. This matters because (1) covert leader-level contact lowers transaction costs for future joint operations, (2) it creates trusted channels for sharing air-defense, targeting, and threat intelligence, and (3) it signals to Iran that retaliation will be met by a coordinated coalition rather than isolated states.

Second, the alliance gives the UAE hard-security capabilities it could not build alone. Three reasons: one, Israel can provide battle-tested missile defense and operational expertise; two, the UAE gains access to a partner with superior intelligence on Iranian networks and missile threats; three, the UAE can use this relationship to hedge against overreliance on Washington, especially when US commitment becomes uncertain under future administrations.

Third, this changes the regional balance by normalizing anti-Iran alignment among Arab states. This matters because it raises the cost of Iranian escalation, encourages other states to quietly cooperate with Israel, and makes it harder for Iran to exploit Arab-Israeli divisions to isolate either side.

opp_args.thesis: The visit exposes a fragile, transactional alliance that deepens regional polarization, increases the risk of escalation with Iran, and ties both governments to unpopular war policies and human-rights abuses.
mechanisms: First, covert military coordination makes the UAE a more obvious target for Iranian retaliation. One, secrecy does not prevent detection once strikes or air-defense transfers become public; two, Iran can respond asymmetrically through proxies, cyberattacks, or attacks on energy infrastructure; three, the UAE's economic model depends on stability, so even limited retaliation imposes outsized costs.

Second, the alliance is politically brittle because it depends on the current US and leadership alignment. One, both Israel and the UAE are vulnerable to a change in Washington's policy direction; two, the relationship is driven by shared threat perception rather than durable public legitimacy; three, once the Iran war ends, domestic and regional pressure may force both sides to distance themselves, limiting long-term strategic value.

Third, the partnership normalizes impunity by linking two governments accused of grave abuses. One, Israel is under ICC arrest warrants and genocide allegations over Gaza; two, the UAE is widely accused of arming the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan; three, closer cooperation gives both sides diplomatic cover and weakens international accountability norms.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether you prioritize immediate deterrence and operational effectiveness or long-term regional stability and legitimacy. Prop wins if the round is about hard security against Iran; opp wins if the clash is about escalation risk, civilian harm, and the fragility of alliances built on secrecy and external patronage.

THBT the Abraham Accords have made the Middle East more stable
THP a world where Gulf states form an explicit anti-Iran security bloc with Israel
THBT states should prioritize covert military alliances over public diplomatic normalization in hostile regions

cards.title: Trump-Aligned Fed Chair Raises Stakes Over US Monetary Independence
cards.background: The US Senate confirmed Kevin Warsh as chair of the Federal Reserve by a 54-45 vote, with Pennsylvania Democrat John Fetterman joining Republicans. Warsh will begin a four-year term as Fed chair on 14 May, alongside a 14-year appointment on the Fed’s rate-setting board, replacing Jerome Powell. The appointment comes as the Trump administration is pressuring the Fed to cut interest rates while inflation has risen to 3.8%, and Powell has said he will remain on the board as a voting governor after his chair term ends.

prop_args.thesis: Installing a chair who is politically aligned with the White House increases the risk of premature rate cuts, which can entrench inflation and weaken the Fed’s credibility.
mechanisms: First, a more politically responsive chair lowers the barrier to easing policy before inflation is fully contained. This is because (1) the chair sets the agenda and frames the internal debate, (2) the White House is explicitly demanding lower rates, and (3) Warsh has already echoed Trump’s call for cuts, so the institutional pressure is no longer abstract.

Second, even if the chair cannot dictate policy alone, they can shift the coalition inside the 12-member voting board. Three reasons: one, the chair controls information flow and meeting priorities; two, markets read the chair as the Fed’s signal of future direction; three, dissenting governors face higher political and reputational costs when the chair is publicly aligned with the president.

Third, the macroeconomic downside of cutting too early is asymmetric. This matters because (1) inflation is already at 3.8%, so easing risks re-accelerating prices, (2) once inflation expectations de-anchor, the Fed must later raise rates more aggressively, and (3) that second-round tightening is more recessionary than waiting would have been.

prop_args.thesis: Warsh’s confirmation threatens the Fed’s institutional independence, which is essential for long-run economic stability and investor confidence.
mechanisms: First, the appointment creates a precedent that monetary policy is a partisan reward rather than a technocratic function. This is because (1) the vote split was almost entirely along party lines, (2) Warsh refused to answer a basic democratic legitimacy question about 2020, and (3) Democrats are already describing him as a Trump 'sock puppet', which signals that future chairs will be judged by loyalty rather than competence.

Second, perceived politicization raises the risk premium on US assets. Three reasons: one, investors price in more policy uncertainty when central bank decisions look politically driven; two, bond markets demand higher yields if inflation discipline is doubted; three, higher yields feed through into mortgages, corporate borrowing, and public debt servicing costs.

Third, the Fed’s ability to act as a crisis backstop depends on trust. This matters because (1) in recessions or financial shocks, the public must believe the Fed will prioritize stability over electoral cycles, (2) if that trust erodes, policy transmission becomes weaker, and (3) the economy becomes more vulnerable to panic and volatility.

opp_args.thesis: Warsh’s confirmation can improve policy by correcting an overly tight Fed and giving markets a chair more willing to support growth without abandoning inflation control.
mechanisms: First, the US economy may benefit from a chair who is more open to rate cuts if growth is slowing. One, higher rates cool spending and hiring, so keeping them elevated too long can unnecessarily raise unemployment; two, Warsh is an experienced former Fed governor and Wall Street economist, so he is not an amateur political appointee; three, a chair who can credibly argue for easing may prevent the Fed from overcorrecting on inflation.

Second, the appointment may restore balance after a period of policy rigidity. One, Warsh previously served on the Fed from 2006 to 2011 and has seen both crisis stimulus and inflation-fighting; two, his earlier reputation as an inflation hawk suggests he is not automatically dovish; three, that combination can produce a more flexible, data-dependent policy mix rather than a one-directional bias.

Third, if inflation is driven partly by external shocks, rate hikes are a blunt tool and cuts may be justified. This is because (1) the article notes war in the Middle East, which can raise energy and supply costs outside the Fed’s control, (2) tighter policy cannot fix supply-side inflation, and (3) maintaining excessively high rates in that environment risks sacrificing jobs for limited disinflation.

opp_args.thesis: The Fed’s institutional structure still constrains any one chair, so fears of capture are overstated.
mechanisms: First, the chair is only one vote on a 12-member rate-setting board. One, Warsh must persuade other governors and regional presidents, not command them; two, the article explicitly says he must convince the board to lower rates; three, that internal veto structure limits any single president’s ability to hijack policy.

Second, public commitments to independence and market scrutiny discipline the chair. One, Warsh told senators he would 'take politics out of monetary policy'; two, any obvious deviation would be punished by markets, Congress, and the Fed’s own professional staff; three, the chair’s credibility is a valuable asset, so even a politically connected chair has incentives to preserve it.

Third, Powell’s continued presence on the board provides continuity and a counterweight. One, Powell is staying on as a voting governor, so the outgoing chair does not disappear immediately; two, that means the board retains institutional memory and an internal check on abrupt policy shifts; three, continuity reduces the chance of a sudden, destabilizing break from prior Fed practice.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether political alignment actually translates into policy capture or whether institutional constraints keep the Fed independent. Prop is stronger on systemic risk and credibility loss; opp is stronger if the round centers on growth and the claim that the Fed has room to ease without reigniting inflation.

THBT central banks should be insulated from elected executives
THP a world where central bank chairs are appointed by legislatures rather than presidents

cards.title: Sticky U.S. Inflation Pushes the Fed Toward a New Hiking Bias
cards.background: Bloomberg reports that the U.S. is seeing its highest inflation in three years, with recent data pushing markets to expect the Federal Reserve will not cut rates soon. Two-year Treasury yields rose to 4%, their highest since June last year, as traders priced in a higher chance that the next Fed move will be a hike rather than a cut. The discussion features Douglas Holtz-Eakin, former CBO director and president of the American Action Forum, assessing how the inflation print will affect Fed rate decisions as Warsh arrives at the central bank debate.

prop_args.thesis: The Fed should prioritize inflation credibility and keep policy tighter for longer, even if that means slower growth in the short run.
mechanisms: First, higher inflation expectations become self-reinforcing if the Fed signals tolerance. This is because (1) households and firms start setting wages and prices around the assumption that inflation will stay elevated, (2) long-term borrowing costs rise as investors demand an inflation premium, and (3) the central bank loses the ability to anchor expectations without a sharper future tightening cycle.

Second, keeping rates elevated protects the Fed's institutional credibility. Three reasons: one, the Fed's core mandate is price stability, so missing on inflation is more damaging than missing modestly on growth; two, markets already moved to price a higher probability of a hike, so easing now would look like capitulation; three, a credible anti-inflation stance reduces the risk of a later Volcker-style shock.

Third, the medium-term welfare loss from inflation is larger than the short-term pain of tighter money. This matters because persistent inflation erodes real wages, disproportionately hurts savers and fixed-income households, and creates policy uncertainty that suppresses productive investment more than a temporary rate hold does.

opp_args.thesis: The Fed should avoid overreacting to a temporary inflation spike because tighter policy risks unnecessary damage to employment and financial stability.
mechanisms: First, rate hikes work with long and variable lags, so reacting to one hot print can overshoot. One, monetary tightening today affects mortgages, business credit, and hiring only after months; two, inflation may already be easing in underlying components even if headline data is high; three, if the Fed hikes into a slowdown, it can create a recession after the inflation shock has passed.

Second, higher rates can trigger broader financial stress. One, two-year Treasury yields at 4% raise funding costs across the economy, including for small firms and leveraged borrowers; two, higher debt-service burdens can expose weak balance sheets and amplify defaults; three, if markets are already volatile, an aggressive Fed move can tighten conditions far beyond what the committee intends.

Third, the Fed should preserve flexibility rather than lock itself into a hawkish path. One, the next move being 'more likely a hike than a cut' is still just market pricing, not a policy necessity; two, the central bank can wait for more data before committing to a direction; three, avoiding premature tightening keeps room to respond if growth weakens or inflation proves transitory.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the inflation shock is persistent enough to justify sacrificing near-term growth for credibility. Prop wins if you think expectations are becoming unanchored and the Fed must prevent a larger future correction; opp wins if you think the data is noisy and the real risk is tightening into a slowdown with long lags.
motion_areas: TH, as the Federal Reserve, would keep interest rates higher for longer despite slowing growth
THBT central banks should prioritize inflation credibility over short-term employment concerns
THP a world where the next Fed move is more likely a hike than a cut

cards.title: China’s Economic Leverage Is Real, But U.S.-Led Allied Coordination Still Decides the Trade War
cards.background: The article discusses the Trump administration’s 2025 tariff escalation against China, including a brief 145 percent tariff spike in April 2025 and an effective tariff rate of around 40 percent for much of the year. China retaliated with equivalent tariffs and used its dominance in rare-earth minerals to threaten U.S. industrial supply chains, forcing Washington into May 14 trade talks seeking relief on rare-earth controls and Chinese purchases of U.S. goods. The piece also cites estimates that U.S. exports to China were around $500 billion in 2024, Chinese exports to the U.S. fell 20 percent in 2025, and China recorded a $1.2 trillion trade surplus.

prop_args.thesis: The United States and its allies still have the stronger long-run economic position, so China’s current leverage is tactical rather than decisive.
mechanisms: First, the U.S.-led bloc controls the highest-value nodes of the global economy. This is because (1) Western firms capture 38 percent of global profits versus 16 percent for China and Hong Kong combined, (2) in high technology the U.S. and allies capture 83.8 percent of global profits while China gets only 6.1 percent, and (3) China’s export machine depends on foreign capital, technology, and market access, so decoupling hurts Beijing’s core growth model more than America’s.

Second, China’s apparent strength is concentrated in a few asymmetric choke points, not broad economic resilience. Three reasons: one, rare earths are a low-value $6 billion industry that can be stockpiled and eventually diversified away; two, China’s leverage works best only in the short run before supply chains adjust; three, most of China’s value-added manufacturing remains in low-tech sectors like metals, plastics, and toys, which are easier to relocate than advanced ecosystem capabilities.

Third, the U.S. can convert structural advantage into real coercive power if it coordinates with allies. This matters because (1) the U.S. bloc’s GDP is more than 2.5 times the China bloc’s GDP, (2) allied coordination magnifies sanctions, export controls, and supply-chain relocation, and (3) a united Western front prevents China from playing one country off against another and reduces the chance that Beijing can veto U.S. policy through selective retaliation.

opp_args.thesis: China has the stronger near-term escalation dominance because it can impose concentrated pain on the U.S. faster and more cheaply than Washington can respond.
mechanisms: First, China’s rare-earth dominance creates an immediate industrial choke point. One, rare-earth inputs are critical for autos, aircraft, and weapons production; two, mines outside China typically take at least a decade to come online, so substitution is not quick; three, Beijing can cut exports at low domestic cost while U.S. firms face immediate assembly-line disruptions.

Second, U.S. retaliation tools are more self-harming and politically harder to sustain. One, financial sanctions and technology cutoffs would hit U.S. companies and consumers as well as China; two, the U.S. has a lower pain threshold because the costs are visible in prices, jobs, and inflation; three, unilateral tariffs are blunt and easy for China to route around by redirecting exports to third markets.

Third, Trump-style alliance fragmentation weakens the West’s structural advantage. One, Europe is drifting toward strategic autonomy after trade conflict and disputes over Greenland and Iran; two, without allied participation the U.S. loses the scale needed to outmuscle China; three, if Washington acts alone, the balance shifts much closer to parity, making Chinese coercion much more effective.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is time horizon: China appears stronger in the short run because rare-earth coercion is immediate and cheap, but the U.S.-led bloc is stronger over a sustained contest because it controls the higher-value parts of the global economy and can mobilize allies. This argument wins because BP debates on trade wars usually hinge on whether temporary pain translates into durable leverage; here, the article itself suggests China’s leverage is real but brittle if the West coordinates.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would pursue coordinated economic decoupling from China
THBT the West should form an economic security alliance to counter Chinese coercion
THP a world where rare-earth supply chains are treated as a national security issue
TH, as the EU, would align with the United States against China despite economic costs
THBT developing nations should resist becoming part of a China-led economic bloc

cards.title: Trump’s Beijing Summit Becomes a Test of Whether China Can Exploit a US-Iran War to Rebalance Great-Power Ties
cards.background: President Donald Trump arrived in Beijing for the first state visit to China by a US leader in nine years, with Air Force One landing at Beijing Capital International Airport slightly before 8 p.m. on Wednesday. The summit comes as the US-Iran conflict remains unresolved and reports suggest Iran may still retain intact missile capabilities. Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, a military honor guard, and hundreds of flag-waving children greeted the president at the airport.

prop_args.thesis: The Iran war gives China leverage to force the US into a more cautious, transactional relationship that weakens Washington’s broader strategic position.
mechanisms: First, the conflict increases US dependence on Chinese cooperation for crisis management. This is because (1) Washington needs Beijing to avoid escalation through diplomacy, sanctions enforcement, or backchannel signaling; (2) China can condition that cooperation on concessions in trade, technology, or Taiwan-related restraint; and (3) the US cannot easily walk away from coordination when a live regional war raises global energy and security risks.

Second, the war distracts and stretches US strategic bandwidth. Three reasons: one, the administration must split attention between the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific; two, military and intelligence resources get diverted toward deterrence and force protection; three, allies see a less focused US and hedge accordingly, which weakens coalition credibility against China.

Third, any perception that Iran still has intact missile capabilities raises the cost of US escalation and makes China look like the more stable great-power interlocutor. This matters because Beijing can present itself as the indispensable manager of order while the US appears reactive, which improves China’s diplomatic standing and bargaining power in the summit.

opp_args.thesis: The Iran war does not fundamentally change the summit because US-China rivalry is structural, and both sides still have strong incentives to stabilize ties.
mechanisms: First, the core US-China relationship is driven by long-term economic and security interdependence, not by one regional war. One, both economies are too large to decouple quickly; two, both governments need predictable trade and market access; three, neither side wants a crisis spiral that damages growth and domestic stability.

Second, China has limited ability to convert the Iran conflict into durable leverage. One, Beijing does not control the battlefield and cannot guarantee outcomes in Iran; two, overt opportunism risks making China look predatory and undermines its image as a responsible power; three, if China pushes too hard, the US can respond with tariffs, export controls, or alliance consolidation.

Third, the summit itself creates a stabilizing channel that lowers the odds of miscalculation. One, leader-level meetings reduce uncertainty and allow direct bargaining; two, both sides can compartmentalize Iran from trade and technology disputes; three, even limited de-escalation is valuable enough that both governments have incentives to keep the relationship from collapsing.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the Iran war creates temporary bargaining leverage or durable structural change. Prop wins if you think crisis dependence and US distraction let China extract concessions now; opp wins if you think the US-China rivalry is too deep to be meaningfully altered by one external conflict and that both sides still prefer stabilization.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would prioritize summit diplomacy with China during an active Middle East war
THBT the US should seek Chinese cooperation in managing Iran even at the cost of concessions elsewhere
THP a world where major power summits occur during ongoing regional wars

cards.title: China Could Trade Hormuz Pressure for US Concessions on Taiwan
cards.region: United States / China / Iran / Taiwan / Strait of Hormuz / Gulf
cards.background: Ahead of a Trump-Xi summit in China, US officials have urged Beijing to help pressure Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz after Tehran’s blockade and a short-lived US military effort to force the waterway open failed in under 48 hours. Analysts quoted in the article say China may be willing to intervene because it imports Iranian and Middle East oil, but only if Washington makes concessions on issues Beijing cares about, especially Taiwan. Trump has said he does not need Xi’s help on Iran, while US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly called on China to join the operation and accused Beijing of helping fund Iran through oil purchases.

prop_args.thesis: The summit gives China leverage to extract concessions on Taiwan by positioning itself as indispensable to resolving the Hormuz crisis.
mechanisms: First, China becomes a gatekeeper on a problem the US cannot solve cheaply on its own. This is because (1) Iran is refusing direct talks while the US naval siege has already failed to restore traffic, (2) China is one of the few actors with enough trade and diplomatic access to pressure Tehran, and (3) Washington’s need for a quick de-escalation rises as petrol prices and inflation worsen domestically.

Second, Beijing can convert that leverage into bargaining power on Taiwan. Three reasons: one, Taiwan is China’s top strategic priority and the issue Beijing is most likely to raise in a summit; two, Trump has not yet signed the $14bn Taiwan arms package, creating a concrete concession point; three, China can ask for softer US language on Taiwanese independence or delays in arms sales without making a formal, irreversible deal.

Third, this matters because it shifts the bilateral balance beyond the immediate Iran file. If the US trades on Taiwan for Hormuz, it signals that pressure on regional flashpoints can be bundled into great-power bargaining, which strengthens China’s broader coercive diplomacy and weakens US credibility with allies that rely on American security guarantees.

prop_args.thesis: China has strong incentives to help reopen Hormuz, but only if it can do so in a way that preserves its image as a diplomatic power rather than a subordinate to US strategy.
mechanisms: First, Beijing has an economic interest in reopening the strait. This is because (1) China is a major importer of Iranian and Middle East oil, (2) its strategic reserves are finite and cannot fully offset a prolonged disruption, and (3) energy shocks would hit Chinese growth and manufacturing costs.

Second, China can use the crisis to present itself as the responsible multilateral actor. Three reasons: one, Xi’s four-point plan emphasizes sovereignty, international law, and diplomacy; two, China has already hosted Iran’s foreign minister and called for a ceasefire and negotiations; three, contrasting itself with Trump’s threats lets Beijing appeal to the Global South and reinforce its “peace broker” branding.

Third, this matters because China can gain reputational and strategic benefits even without a formal quid pro quo. By appearing helpful on Iran while avoiding direct alignment with US coercion, Beijing can improve ties with Gulf states, reduce energy risk, and still keep Taiwan as a separate bargaining chip for later.

opp_args.thesis: China is unlikely to make meaningful concessions on Taiwan because the Iran crisis is too peripheral to justify compromising its core sovereignty claim.
mechanisms: First, Taiwan is existential for Beijing while Hormuz is only instrumental. One, the Chinese Communist Party frames Taiwan as a core sovereignty issue, not a negotiable foreign-policy preference; two, any concession on arms sales or anti-independence language risks domestic backlash and signals weakness; three, China can tolerate short-term oil pain better than it can tolerate a precedent of bargaining over territorial claims.

Second, Beijing has alternative ways to manage the Iran shock without paying a Taiwan price. One, it can draw on strategic oil reserves and reroute imports; two, it can continue quiet diplomacy with Tehran and the Gulf without openly siding with Washington; three, it can wait for the US operation to fail or stall, which would reduce the need for a deal.

Third, this means the summit is more likely to produce symbolic cooperation than substantive trade-offs. China can issue statements calling for restraint and safe passage through Hormuz while refusing any real shift on Taiwan, because that lets it look constructive without sacrificing its long-term strategic position.

opp_args.thesis: The US has too much to lose from linking Iran policy to Taiwan, so Trump is more likely to resist Chinese demands than to concede.
mechanisms: First, making Taiwan part of the Iran bargain would alarm US allies and undermine deterrence in Asia. One, Japan, the Philippines, and Taiwan itself read US arms sales and rhetoric as signals of commitment; two, any perceived softness on Taiwan encourages Chinese coercion in the Strait; three, the US would be seen as trading away a democratic partner for a temporary energy fix.

Second, Trump has domestic and strategic reasons not to pay that price. One, he has already framed the Iran crisis as under control and may not want to look dependent on Xi; two, the Republican base is hawkish on China and could punish concessions on Taiwan; three, the administration may prefer coercion against Iran to avoid appearing to reward Beijing’s leverage.

Third, this means China’s leverage may be overstated. If Washington can find other ways to reopen Hormuz or simply absorb the costs, Beijing’s bargaining position weakens, and the summit becomes a theater for rivalry rather than a real exchange of concessions.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether China’s leverage over Hormuz is strong enough to force a trade on Taiwan, or whether Taiwan’s status is too central for Beijing to bargain away. This argument wins because the US has urgent short-term pressure from energy markets, but China has the stronger structural advantage: it can offer a useful service while keeping any Taiwan concession vague, symbolic, or delayed.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would not link Taiwan policy to cooperation on Iran
THBT the US should trade limited concessions on Taiwan for Chinese help reopening Hormuz
THP a world where great powers can condition crisis cooperation on unrelated strategic concessions
THBT China should use energy security leverage to force US restraint on Taiwan

cards.title: Nepal’s Internet Boom Masks a Rural Affordability Trap That Locks Millions Out of the Digital Economy
cards.background: Nepal’s telecom regulator reported broadband penetration of 145.69% in early 2026, but independent estimates put actual internet use much lower: DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Nepal report said only 56% of the population was online in late 2025, leaving roughly 13 million people offline. The Nepal Living Standards Survey 2022/23 found only about 40% of households had internet at home, while just 9.5% of households below the poverty line were connected. The gap is especially severe in rural provinces such as Karnali, where internet penetration is around 14%, compared with 79.3% in the Kathmandu Valley.

prop_args.thesis: Nepal’s current internet model is a regressive system that deepens inequality because market-led expansion reaches profitable users while excluding poor, rural, and socially marginalized communities.
mechanisms: First, the market only serves dense and high-demand areas, so providers rationally avoid remote villages. This is because (1) Nepal Telecom officials say expansion usually happens only when there are 100 to 200 potential users, (2) rural terrain makes infrastructure expensive to build and maintain, and (3) low user density means firms cannot recover fixed costs without subsidies.

Second, the price people pay is not the real issue; the problem is that poor-quality service makes internet effectively unusable. Three reasons: one, households below the poverty line have only 9.5% internet access, two, users in places like Baitadi pay 1,000–1,500 rupees monthly for unstable connections, and three, frequent outages, weak signals, and failed transactions mean the service cannot support education, payments, or work.

Third, unequal access compounds existing caste, gender, and education gaps, turning connectivity into a privilege rather than a public good. This matters because (1) only 41% of Nepali women use the internet, (2) higher-caste households have 37% access versus 21% for Dalit households, and (3) people with master’s degrees are far more likely to be online than those with only secondary education, so digital exclusion reproduces offline hierarchy.

opp_args.thesis: Nepal’s internet problem is primarily a rollout and literacy challenge, not a failure of affordability, so the right fix is infrastructure expansion and user support rather than treating the market as fundamentally broken.
mechanisms: First, headline penetration and fiber growth show that access is improving quickly, so the state should focus on completion rather than redesign. One, Nepal Telecom has extended fiber to all 77 districts, two, the Rural Telecommunications Development Fund has connected over 16,000 public sites, and three, the IFC and World Bank are already injecting capital into the sector, meaning the bottleneck is implementation, not absence of investment.

Second, many users underutilize existing networks because digital literacy and household setup are weak. This is because (1) digital literacy is only 31%, (2) some connection failures are caused by router placement or internal wiring rather than the network itself, and (3) content is often only in Nepali or English, so even connected users may not convert access into meaningful use.

Third, internet prices are not uniquely unaffordable in comparative terms, so the political focus on cost can be misleading. Three reasons: one, industry leaders argue Nepal has some of the cheapest internet in the world, two, mobile broadband is widely available and subscriptions are high, and three, the real issue is value and reliability rather than nominal price, meaning targeted regulation and education can solve the problem without overcorrecting against the market.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether internet access is treated as a consumer good or as essential infrastructure. Prop wins if the round is about who is actually excluded from participation in education, finance, and jobs, because the data shows the poorest and rural users are structurally left behind; Opp wins if the round is about policy feasibility, since Nepal already has expanding infrastructure and the remaining gap is partly literacy and last-mile implementation.
